name: Plum
lede: Plum is the reddish purple of a ripe plum's skin, a color word that naturalists were using by the early 1800s and that the web now uses for two quite different colors.

sections.title: Two plums on the web
sections.body:
*Plum* names the purple of the fruit, with a lean toward red; Paterson's dictionary glosses it as a reddish purple [1]. The same entry points out that the X11 color list, the source of the web's named colors, also has a Plum, hex #DDA0DD [1]. That one is a pale pink-violet, far lighter than the fruit.

Our swatch is the deeper color, #8E4585, and it sits within a CIEDE2000 distance of 5.2 of the ISCC-NBS 1955 block called strong reddish purple [2]. The 2010 xkcd color survey has its own Plum at #580F41, much darker, while its Light Eggplant lies within a distance of 1.2 of ours [2]. Of the colors with articles here, [[purple]] is the parent, and [[eggplant]], [[mauve]] and [[orchid]] are the nearest named relatives in hue.

The record of the word is short. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists plum as a color from 1805 [2], and the German RAL system carried a matching Signal Violet, number 4008, by 1927 [2].

sections.title: From plum blue to plum purple
sections.body:
Plum entered the naturalists' colour lists through mineralogy. In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a vocabulary of 54 colors for identifying minerals, and he and his students kept revising it for roughly forty years [3]. Werner's list and the one by his Scottish follower Robert Jameson called this color *plum blue* [3].

In 1814 the Scottish painter Patrick Syme expanded the list to 108 names, and to 110 in 1821 [3]. He made purple and orange principal colors, so Werner's plum blue became *plum purple* [3]. Syme gave it the number 42, and for his examples he named the skin of a plum and the mineral fluor spar [4].

Syme also gave a recipe, marked as Werner's: mostly Berlin blue and carmine red, with a trace of brown and the faintest touch of black [4]. Berlin blue is the older name of [[prussian-blue]], and the red is [[carmine]], so the naturalists' plum was blue first and red second. A modern edition adds the wing feathers of the spectacled cormorant as an animal example [4]. It also warns that Syme's swatches have grown more muted with age, so the printed plum is a pale ghost of what he painted [3]. The nearby slug [[plum-purple]] is the dark successor name in our library.

sections.title: The bloom on the skin
sections.body:
A plum is not one flat purple. Samuel Johnson's dictionary defined *bloom* as the blue colour upon plums and grapes newly gathered, and Paterson records the definition [5]. The same book defines *glaucous* partly as covered with a bloom in the way a plum is [5]. That waxy film cools the skin and lightens it, and wiping it off with a thumb shows the redder, darker color beneath.

Medieval writers noticed the fruit's change too. Pastoureau notes that fruit was thought of as green first, then red (cherries, strawberries), then blue or black (plums, blackberries, blueberries), a ripening that stood for freshness [6].

sections.title: What the plum tree dyed
sections.body: The plum tree did not give the Romans purple [7]. Pastoureau lists black plum and plum leaves among the long-used materials of Roman dyers' greens, alongside ferns and leek juice [7]. He adds elsewhere that plant greens, black plum among them, held up badly as painters' colors [7]. For the color we call plum, they used other sources, among them the shellfish purple of [[tyrian-purple]].

sections.title: In paint, skin and speech
sections.body:
Painters built plum colors in layers. Ball describes a cloak of plum red that Jan Gossaert, a Flemish painter of the 1500s, built from red lake laid over dark grey, as microscope sections show [8]. The color is made in the eye, from a transparent red over a dark underlayer, and not by mixing a purple pigment.

The word also turns up where nobody expects it. A traveller's account quoted by Balfour-Paul describes skin worked on by indigo, sun and oil as taking a bloom of deep plum, neither brown nor blue [9]. In 1827 the Nuremberg dermatologist Heinrich Eichhorn listed a plum shade of purple among the colors he wanted doctors to name in skin disease [10], and Birren's survey describes Osler's disease as leaving the face brick red or plum color in warm weather [11].

Paterson passes on a tentative suggestion that the English *livid*, once black-and-blue like a bruise, may be linked to the Old Slavonic *sliva*, a plum [12]. The same entry gives the Latin *lividus* as the source, so treat the plum link as a guess [12]. Paterson notes that Professor Plum is the last surviving colour surname among the six original suspects in the board game Cluedo [13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, this plum, within CIEDE2000 4, covers 1% of the canvas in none, and appears at all in 1 painting, as photographed [14]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and the photographs are of aged, varnished pictures. A saturated reddish purple is a rare thing in old paint, and Gossaert's cloak shows one reason: a painter's plum was usually a dark glaze, which a camera records as dark red or brown [8][14].

In printed English, the adjective use of *plum*, which is the color sense, peaks in the 1860s and rose fastest in the 1820s, and the word in all senses peaks in the 1890s [15]. The 1820s rise matches the years when Syme's color lists were in the hands of naturalists [3][15]. That timing may be coincidence, and the data cannot test it.

questions.q: In Patrick Syme's color system, what natural example did he give for Plum Purple?
Which colour did dyers of the first century CE get from black plum and plum leaves, according to Pastoureau?
True or false: the web's X11 Plum (#DDA0DD) is the same deep color as the fruit.

openers: Look for the pale bloom on a plum's skin: Samuel Johnson called it the blue upon the fruit, and it is why a plum looks cooler than it is.
Naturalists called this color plum blue before Patrick Syme renamed it plum purple, in 1814.
The plum tree supplied Roman dyers with green, not purple.

issues: Pastoureau dye/paint greens: dyers' materials 'long used'; 'held up badly' applies to painters only
Balfour-Paul quote wording: neither brown nor blue
Birren plum face = Osler's disease, not general diagnostic tables
